Morgan opens the Session Option Brief. It says the free session is a good idea. The wording sounds settled. Yet the brief has only prepared a comparison. Somebody still has to decide whether the proposal belongs on next month's program agenda. A recommendation can make that decision easier to reach. It cannot quietly become the decision itself.

Today we put the decision in the center. Ask one question: ‘Should Morgan propose one free digital-skills session to the program team for next month?’ That is narrower than ‘run a workshop.’ It has a named owner, real alternatives, and a next step that can be held. Morgan can propose the session, request another option, or decline for now. The agent may compare evidence and recommend a path. Morgan owns the call and the explanation.

What if the answer is wrong? A false claim about room capacity could waste a facilitator's preparation. A false attendance signal could make the team spend scarce time on a session nobody asked for. Even in the Harbor case, the wrong number sends work to people who did not choose it. That is why the card records reversibility. Morgan can withdraw an internal proposal. A public announcement or a paid booking would be harder to unwind, and neither is in scope here.

List the evidence the owner would need: a current room-capacity note, an attendance summary with a clear time window, and facilitator availability for the proposed date. Each item must have a source ID and freshness check. If one is missing, the brief can show the gap. It cannot turn a guess into a fact. The agent's allowed actions are to read those cleared notes, draft alternatives, and place the brief in a review folder. It may not put a date on a calendar, contact participants, or commit money.

Now write the stop condition before you write the best-case path. If the capacity note is stale, if the facilitator has not confirmed availability, or if the sources disagree, mark the recommendation ‘hold for Morgan.’ A confidence score can help triage; it cannot replace the named gate. For this classroom card, we use a simple rule: all three required source IDs must be present and current before a recommendation appears. Even then, Morgan decides.

Pause on your own workflow. What choice is a human accountable for after the agent prepares its work?

Fill the Decision Card now. Write the choice, the owner, three alternatives, the evidence, the agent's preparation scope, forbidden execution, and the condition that sends the work back to a person. Add the consequence of a wrong answer. If you find that one card contains three separate decisions, split it. A single approval button cannot make three different responsibilities disappear.

Put the card into your Operating File as a draft. Stop if you cannot name one accountable owner or if the agent can approve its own recommendation. In the next lesson, we will make the evidence path readable to that owner.

expected_output.scope: one complete lesson, all eight exact canonical narration rows
expected_output.format: single continuous lossless or high-quality audio master with timing/transcript receipt
expected_output.duration: script estimate only; verify native duration and sentence alignment before local composite
expected_output.captions: regenerate from exact words after audio alignment; desktop and 390x844 contextual MP4 review required
expected_output.presenter: preserve existing native presenter footage and audio at normal speed/pitch; avoid double speech

input_limits.gate: verify documented single-job character limit and output duration before any request; stop if insufficient

privacy_rights.inputs: canonical synthetic workshop script only; omit real participant records and secret IDs

cost_request.gate: obtain exact metered price, fees and enforceable aggregate cap before seeking separate execution authority; stop if total cannot be capped below ceiling
